label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
# Cup Day, the Coolroom, and Why You Should Have Been There

Jonno, you've been messaging me for three weeks asking what happened on Cup Day. You saw my story, you know something went down, and you've been too nosy to leave it alone. So here it is, all of it, in one place, so you can stop texting me "wait WHAT" every four hours. Enjoy it from your flat in London, where it's probably raining and you're probably eating a sad sandwich.

It started Monday night. The coolroom compressor just quit. No warning, no dramatic noise, it just gave up like a bloke on a Friday arvo at his mate's wedding. Nobody knew until Tuesday morning, when I rolled in at 6.40am on Cup Day and opened the door to find the thermometer sitting at 11 degrees. Eleven. Bro. That's a coolroom having a nap on a bed of crushed dreams.

Now, you know what Cup Day lunch is like. We had 140 covers booked, three-course set menu, the whole room full of people in fascinators and dodgy hats, and we were looking at the rest of the day with a coolroom that was basically a warm cupboard full of expensive protein.

I rang Wally from Coldline. Wally said he'd come Wednesday because the part was coming from Sydney, and Wally said it like he was doing us a massive favour. "Wednesday's the earliest, mate." Cheers, Wal. Cheers for that.

So Phil, the owner, turns up at about 7 with his coffee and his face, and he goes, "Just make it work, mate." Which, for the record, is not a plan. That is a sentence people say when they want the problem to go away and they'd like to be somewhere else. I love Phil, but Phil has never once had to figure out where 30 kilos of dairy goes when the coolroom is a crime scene.

So we made it work. Everything got moved. Two undercounters, the bar fridge, and Marta's cafe next door let us use half her walk-in, which is the most generous thing anyone's done for us all year, and which she has now used as leverage to get three weeks of my staff meal in croissant credit. I owe her three weeks. I'm eating Marta's pastries until I die, and honestly, I'm not even mad.

Raff was off that day, so it was me running the pass. Which, if you remember, is the exact position I've spent years being nervous about. Turns out when you have no other option, you just do it, and you do it while sweating through your shirt and pretending you know what you're doing.

We lost about $1800 worth of stock in the end. Mostly dairy, and the duck legs. The duck legs, Jonno. I was looking at a tray of confit duck legs in the bin like they'd died in my arms. Actually, it's more that I looked at them, then looked at the clock, then said a short prayer and walked away.

Then came the beef shin.

Me and Benny had to get 30 kilos of beef shin from the walk-in next door down the laneway, because it was raining, obviously, and we didn't have any other way to move it. We used a milk crate on a trolley. A milk crate. On a trolley. Halfway down the laneway, one of the wheels just fell off. Just dropped off, rolled away like it had had enough of us, and we're standing there in the rain with a crate full of beef, going, "Mate, what do we do?" And Benny just looks at me, dead serious, and goes, "We carry it." So we carried it. Thirty kilos of shin, two blokes, one wheel on a milk crate, and not a single one of us dropped it. I'm very proud of that, and I'm also deeply unhappy about it.

Kev, our dishy, filled the old esky with ice from the servo down the road. Fourteen bags. Fourteen. The servo guy asked if we were having a party. Kev said, "Yeah, mate, a party for the beef." The servo guy just nodded like that made complete sense, which it did, because everything that day made sense in a completely insane way.

And then we had to 86 the panna cotta at 12.15. Panna cotta. We had 140 people in the room and we ran out of panna cotta. So dessert became "affogato with whatever," which was basically a bunch of coffee and whatever ice cream we could get our hands on, and honestly, people loved it more. I don't know how that happened. I'm still processing it. Table after table was asking for seconds like we'd invented the concept of dessert.

There was also a lady on table 9 who asked me, very seriously, whether the beef was "free range from the laneway," because she'd seen us out the window with the milk crate. I said, "Yep, it's a very special cut." I don't know what that means. Neither does she. She ate it. She was happy.

Oh, and my horse in the sweep? Ice Cold Lad. Came second last. Second last, Jonno. The universe is clearly taking the piss, and it's doing it with a horse named after my own nickname for how I feel on a Tuesday.

But here's the thing I actually want you to hear, because you'd never let me hear the end of it if I didn't say it: best service we did all year. Easily. Everyone was locked in. Nobody sooked. Nobody sulked. Benny was carrying shin like a champion, Kev was ice-bag-ing like a gladiator, the girls out front were making every table feel like they'd planned the menu themselves. We were making it up as we went, and we were doing it well, which is the most bistro thing you can possibly do. Bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite, mate. We had both, in massive quantities.

Anyway. You'd have lost your mind. You'd have been out the back shouting at the coolroom, and then you'd have been out the front shouting at the wine list, and then you'd have started a conga line with the milk crate. You would have been an absolute menace and I would have loved it.

Also, you're soft now. London has made you soft. I know you're going to say you're not, but you are. You'd have cried when the duck legs went in the bin. You'd have cried when the horse came in second last. I'm not even joking, you'd have cried.

So that's the story. That's what happened on Cup Day. Now you know, you can stop asking, and you can start planning the trip home. There's a spot at the pass waiting for you, a coolroom that may or may not be working, and a Phil who will definitely still be saying "just make it work, mate."

Come home ya flog.
